extracted.subtask_description: Practical and ethical guidance for novelists and critics: what makes fiction endure, how to craft character and plot, professional habits for productivity, and the duties and proper conduct of critics and authors toward one another.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enduring_novel_quality:_humanity_of_characters
rubrics_metrics.description: Novels endure when the men and women depicted are human in their aspirations, human in their sympathies, and human in their actions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples given: Jane Eyre, Esmond, Adam Bede will outlast works that rely on topicality or artifice (e.g., Pickwick). The implication is that truthful, sympathetic, and realistically motivated characters make a work timeless.

rubrics_metrics.name: Natural_realism_over_sensational_circumstance
rubrics_metrics.description: Human life depicted as natural and real is valuable even if the circumstances are not sensational.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Villette and Shirley are noted as containing 'human life as natural and as real' though their circumstances are less overtly interesting than other novels—showing that realism of character and life can compensate for less dramatic plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Literary_honesty_vs_passing_off_others'_work
rubrics_metrics.description: The sin in literary conduct is not merely taking another's property but passing off as one's own creation that which one did not create.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If an author uses another's language, plot, or dialogue, he should acknowledge it; buying a plot or adapting material does not justify presenting the result as wholly one's own. Examples: Charles Reade's unacknowledged adaptation and uncredited use of Swift's dialogue; advice is to give proper attribution and avoid pretending ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Understand_your_subject_before_attacking_it
rubrics_metrics.description: When a novelist sets out to expose an abuse or vice, he must truly understand his subject or risk misrepresenting it and alienating readers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors who write with earnest purpose but without true comprehension can leave readers sympathizing with those whom the author intended to condemn; thorough understanding prevents unfair or crude portrayals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plotting_styles:_meticulous_construction_vs_organic_writing
rubrics_metrics.description: There are different valid approaches to plotting: meticulous, pre-planned construction (e.g., Wilkie Collins) versus a more organic, discovery-driven method.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meticulous plotting—planning every detail and 'dove-tailing'—can produce wonderful constructions but may remind readers of the mechanism and reduce pleasure for some tastes. Authors should be aware of how visible their plotting appears to readers and choose a method suitable to their aims/audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character_truth_and_dialogue_authenticity
rubrics_metrics.description: Characters should be true to human nature and speak as real people do; dialogue must make personages 'stand upright on the ground.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: Annie Thackeray's sweet, true characters; Rhoda Broughton's energetic characters and realistic speech (e.g., Nancy calling her brother 'You beast!'). Avoid wooden, mawkish, or socially implausible behaviour unless deliberately justified by character or context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_artifice_and_pasteboard_grandeur
rubrics_metrics.description: Fiction should avoid artificial grandeur, tinsel splendour, and stage-properties that create paint-and-unreality impressions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disraeli's novels are criticized for a 'flavour of paint and unreality'—authors should aim for authenticity rather than false glamour that may mislead readers or fail to do moral good.

rubrics_metrics.name: Purpose_of_the_modern_critic
rubrics_metrics.description: A critic's proper objects are (1) to tell the public whether a book is worth public attention, and (2) to describe its purport so readers can learn its contents without reading it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good concise description serves readers who lack time; critics are not always required to be profound philosophers but should be honest and useful summarizers and guides.

rubrics_metrics.name: Critical_honesty_and_impartiality
rubrics_metrics.description: Critics must tell the reader what they actually think; when they write what they do not think (from friendship or animosity) there should be no pardon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid giving praise or censure for improper motives; examples of corruption include accepting presents or favouring acquaintances. Readers have a right to demand honesty even if deep critical ability is not always available.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid_influence_and_touting_for_praise
rubrics_metrics.description: Authors should not run after critics, editors, or gatekeepers seeking praise—such behaviour is disgraceful and debases literature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical examples: sending presents, flattering editors or library keepers, lobbying for positive notice; such practices corrupt both public counsel and the author's dignity, and are unlikely to bring substantial reward.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintaining_distance_between_author_and_critic
rubrics_metrics.description: There should be no intercourse at all between an author and his critic: the critic, as critic, should not know his author, nor the author his critic.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The relationship should avoid quid pro quo influences; praise should not create gratitude that compromises critique, nor should censure provoke anger. Authors should accept criticism as something beyond their influence.

rubrics_metrics.name: When_to_answer_criticism:_only_for_honourable_injury
rubrics_metrics.description: An author should not answer ordinary criticism or quarrel with reviewers; only if a critic makes an assertion injurious to the author's honour (falsehood or discreditable personal motives) is an answer warranted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retaliatory answers, threats, or public sputtering do harm to the author's dignity and public perception; if compelled to respond to injurious falsehoods, do so cautiously and with clean hands.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical_limitations_of_periodical_criticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Much modern criticism is done by paid reviewers who must measure labour by payment; thus readers cannot expect philosophical analysis from every review.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Readers should treat periodical praise/censure as a practical guide: books praised by widely-respected periodicals are more worth attention than books that are ignored. Use reviews to build a quick, if shallow, working knowledge of current literature.

rubrics_metrics.name: Daily_work_routine_and_productivity_target
rubrics_metrics.description: A disciplined daily routine: three hours a day is enough for literary work if the writer can work continuously.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical regimen described: rise early (example: 5:30 A.M.), begin by reading the previous day's work for ~30 minutes to catch tone, then write continuously aiming for 250 words every quarter-hour (use a watch). Read what is written at least twice before sending to the printer. This routine can yield ~10 pages a day and sustained output across months.

rubrics_metrics.name: Train_yourself_to_write_continuously
rubrics_metrics.description: Writers should tutor their minds to avoid idle nibbling and hesitation and be able to work uninterrupted during designated hours.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Discipline and habit (timed word quotas, early hours, reading previous work before resuming) are recommended to make each writing session productive; paying attention to the sound of words and avoiding excessive self-interruption are advised.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plot_plausibility_and_authoral_honesty_about_limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Plots should be plausible and the author should guard against improbable devices; acknowledge limitations in constructing intricate unravellings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authorial self-critique: example of disbelief that Mr. Crawley could forget how he came by a cheque; recognize when a plot mechanism strains credulity and either revise or be candid about its weakness. The author admits personal limits in constructing certain types of intricate plots.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publication_format_and_market_considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: The mode and price of publication affect a novel's commercial success (e.g., sixpenny monthly numbers vs shilling magazines).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Serial and pricing strategies influence reader willingness to buy standalone parts; authors and publishers should consider market formats and how competing periodicals affect sales of novels published in numbers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Character_reuse_and_reader_fatigue
rubrics_metrics.description: Frequent reintroduction of the same characters across works can provoke reader criticism and fatigue.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Be aware that readers and reviewers may complain about recurring figures (archdeacons, dukes); consider fresh characters or justify recurrence, and be prepared to act on criticism if it affects your creative choices (author's anecdote: killing Mrs. Proudie).
